analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare hospitals to maintain safe registered-nurse staffing levels and post staffing information publicly.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 47 cosponsors, including 9 Republicans, but never received a hearing or vote and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every hospital that participates in Medicare to set up a staffing system ensuring enough registered nurses on each shift and in each unit. It would have required hospitals to post daily staffing counts where patients can see them, submit the data to the federal government for public posting, keep records, face civil fines of up to $10,000 per knowing violation, and barred hospitals from punishing patients or nurses who complained about staffing.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients, who would be cared for by better-staffed nursing teams; and registered nurses, who would get a say in staffing plans, whistleblower protection against retaliation, and the right to sue and win reinstatement and back pay if punished for raising staffing complaints.

how_it_helps.text: Each Medicare-participating hospital would have to adopt a staffing system ensuring enough registered nurses on every shift and unit, based on patient numbers and intensity of care, with input from direct-care nurses [S3].

Hospitals would have to post daily, in a clearly visible place, the number of licensed and unlicensed nursing staff on each unit, and the Health and Human Services Department would publish the submitted staffing data on its website [S3].
Hospitals could face civil money penalties of up to $10,000 per knowing violation, with higher penalties for a pattern of violations, and violators' names would be published online [S3].
Nurses who face retaliation for staffing complaints could sue in federal court for reinstatement and lost wages, and patients could win $5,000 in liquidated damages plus attorney's fees [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which would bear the cost of hiring more registered nurses, daily public postings, recordkeeping, data submission, and potential fines. Those costs would ultimately flow through hospital budgets to insurers, Medicare, and patients.

drawbacks.text: The bill's own findings note a critical national shortage of registered nurses; mandating staffing levels during a shortage could force hospitals to compete for scarce nurses or leave requirements unmet [S3].

Compliance costs — more nurses, daily postings, recordkeeping, and data systems — would fall on hospitals, including financially strained rural and safety-net facilities, and would pass through to insurers and government payers [S3].

The bill relies on flexible, hospital-designed staffing systems rather than fixed minimum ratios, which critics of this approach argue leaves too much discretion to hospital management, though it bars using the ratios as an upper limit and requires them to exceed any state law minimums [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Research cited in the bill's findings links registered-nurse staffing levels directly to patient outcomes, and the potential benefit — fewer falls, infections, drug errors, and deaths — is substantial against a cost that is essentially a hospital labor and administration expense. The design is flexible rather than a rigid ratio mandate, which reduces the risk of unrealistic requirements, though a nurse shortage makes compliance genuinely hard for some hospitals. On balance the public benefit likely outweighs the cost, which is precisely why the hospital industry historically opposed such mandates.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee in November 2007, sent to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee ten days later, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2009 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Lois Capps, herself a former nurse, introduced the bill on November 9, 2007, and 47 House members — 38 Democrats and 9 Republicans — signed on as cosponsors [S4].
The Speaker referred it to two committees, Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means, meaning it needed action in at least one of them to move [S5].
On November 19, 2007, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, the last action ever taken on the bill [S5].
No hearing or markup was ever scheduled, and the bill died in committee when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare-participating hospitals came out ahead: they avoided mandatory nurse staffing systems, daily public staffing disclosures, federal data reporting, civil fines, and whistleblower lawsuits. Nurses and hospital patients gained nothing, and unsafe staffing levels continued unaddressed at the federal level.

for.name: Lois Capps
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Registered Nurse Safe Staffing Act of 2007 in the House.

for.name: 47 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan support.

for.name: National nurses' organizations and labor unions
for.what_they_did: Publicly pushed for federal nurse staffing ratios during this era; the bill itself gives unions a formal role in staffing committees.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of primary referral (Chair: John Dingell, D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after referring it to the Health Subcommittee.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Secondary committee of referral (Chair: Charles Rangel, D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; it remained with the committee's jurisdiction untouched.

against.name: Hospital industry
against.what_they_did: Historically opposed federal nurse staffing mandates as costly and inflexible; no such opposition appears in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan — 38 Democrats and 9 Republicans — but with a Democratic House majority and Democratic committee chairs, the bill never advanced past subcommittee referral, so the obstruction came from within the majority party rather than from a partisan floor fight.

industries.note: Hospitals would have to fund more nurse hours, daily public staffing postings, three-year recordkeeping, quarterly data submission, and risk fines up to $10,000 per knowing violation. Because Medicare pays hospitals fixed amounts per stay, added staffing costs would come out of hospital margins rather than being directly reimbursed.

Nurses would gain a formal role in setting staffing levels, whistleblower protections with the right to sue for reinstatement and back pay, and staffing data collection covering injuries, overtime, and turnover.
Better staffing could reduce nursing-sensitive complications like infections and readmissions that insurers pay for, but hospitals might seek higher payment rates to cover staffing costs.
